newsitem.title: USA: Jett wins NASD ruling against Kidder Peabody.
newsitem.headline: Jett wins NASD ruling against Kidder Peabody.

text.p: Joseph Jett, a former Kidder, Peabody & Co. bond trader who allegedly created $348 million in false profits, won a key ruling in his arbitration case against the company Thursday.

The National Association of Securities Dealers denied all claims by Kidder Peabody seeking a monetary award against Jett and directed that the company immediately release $1 million in Jett's account to him, according to a Jett spokesman.
The funds have been frozen in his accounts since Jett was fired by Kidder in 1994.

The remaining balance out of a total of $5.3 million in Jett's account will be held by Kidder Peabody pending a panel's decision on the issue of attorney's fees. The parties are to appear before the panel Jan. 23.
"This is a wonderful victory," Jett's attorney, Kenneth Warner, said in a statement. "An innocent man who has been wrongly accused for nearly three years has now had his name cleared."
The $5.3 million in Jett's account were bonuses Jett accrued between the time he joined Kidder Peabody in July 1991 and the time he left in April 1994.
Kidder was owned by General Electric Co. before its assets were sold to PaineWebber Group Inc.

Although the NASD ordered the release of the $1 million in Jett's account, it denied his claims of deferred compensation, punitive damages and a further interim award for advancement of attorneys' fees.
Kidder Peabody General Counsel John Liftin said Jett had sought $2.8 million in deferred compensation.
"Really what this award seems to do primarily is to deny both sides' requests for relief," Liftin said. He said the award was an interim decision rather than a final one.
Both Kidder and Jett filed for arbitration to resolve their dispute.
Although the NASD ruling is a victory for Jett, the finding does not completely clear the trader. He still faces a civil administrative case filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission.
An administrative hearing was held during the spring, and a ruling by the judge is not expected for several months. An SEC spokeswoman said the NASD ruling does not affect the commission's case.

The SEC alleged Jett concocted fake profits to hide nearly $100 million in losses. The SEC charges involve the way that Jett recorded the profits on Kidder's trading system for the sale of government strips, or securities that are created by peeling away and repackaging the interest payments of 30-year government bonds.

Jett allegedly entered into forward contracts that involved the exchange at a later date of strips for bonds. The SEC alleged that Jett should have settled the contracts when they came due rather than recording profits on "day one".

He has maintained his innocence and in June he testified that his superiors at Kidder knew about his strategy, that they had supported him and that the accounting department concluded his profits were not phony.
